Graduate research report

Wnt/β-catenin target genes and skeletal gene programmes in a mouse craniofacial bone mutant

A results-level transcriptomic analysis of a 4 control versus 4 mutant RNA-seq experiment, interpreted against the TCF/LEF-dependent and TCF/LEF-independent target classes of Doumpas et al. (2019)

Analysis in R 4.6.1 with limma and edgeR 4.10.5. Code and data layout: github.com/mtariqi/craniofacial-wnt-rnaseq (private).

Abstract

Background. Canonical Wnt/β-catenin signalling controls osteoblast commitment, bone mass and craniofacial patterning, and is thought to act almost entirely through the TCF/LEF transcription factors. Doumpas et al. (2019) challenged this by deleting all four TCF/LEF genes in HEK293T cells and identifying β-catenin targets that are regulated without TCF/LEF. Whether these target classes are altered in skeletal tissue in vivo is unknown.

Methods. A DESeq2 results table from a mouse RNA-seq experiment (4 control, 4 mutant; 22,444 genes) was re-analysed. Because raw counts were not available, false discovery rates were recomputed and a signed z-statistic was derived for each gene. Competitive gene set tests (limma cameraPR) were applied to eight Wnt target sets derived from Doumpas et al. and to seven curated craniofacial, cartilage, bone and control gene sets. Concordance between the mutant response and the published CHIR99021 response was assessed by rank correlation.

Results. The expression profile identified the tissue as mineralised bone. Thirty genes were differentially expressed at FDR < 0.05 (25 lower, 5 higher in the mutant). The dominant signal was a coordinated loss of epithelial and keratinocyte transcripts (23-gene set, median log2FC −3.6). Osteoblast (FDR 1×10⁻⁷), osteocyte (FDR 0.002) and osteoclast (FDR 0.003) gene sets were modestly and uniformly higher in the mutant (median log2FC +0.25 to +0.31), whereas Bmp6 was significantly lower (log2FC −0.73, FDR 1×10⁻⁴). None of the Wnt target sets was significantly shifted, canonical readouts (Axin2, Lef1, Nkd1, Dkk1) were unchanged, and the mutant response did not correlate with the published β-catenin response (Spearman ρ −0.21 to 0.15, all p > 0.3).

Conclusions. At the level of bulk tissue there is no evidence that the mutation alters canonical TCF/LEF-mediated Wnt/β-catenin transcription or engages TCF/LEF-independent β-catenin targets. The skeletal signal is best explained by a shift in tissue composition towards mineralised bone, with Bmp6 as the most specific candidate for follow-up. Access to per-sample counts is required to separate composition from biology.

1. Introduction

1.1 Wnt/β-catenin signalling in the skeleton and face

In the absence of Wnt ligands, cytoplasmic β-catenin is phosphorylated by a destruction complex containing Axin, APC, GSK3 and CK1, and degraded. Wnt binding to Frizzled and LRP5/6 inhibits this complex, so β-catenin accumulates, enters the nucleus and, in the canonical model, binds the TCF/LEF transcription factors (TCF7, LEF1, TCF7L1 and TCF7L2) to activate target genes such as Axin2, Nkd1, Sp5 and Dkk1.

This pathway is central to skeletal biology. Genetic studies in mice showed that β-catenin in skeletal progenitors pushes cells towards the osteoblast lineage and away from chondrocyte fate (Day et al., 2005; Hill et al., 2005), and that it is needed for osteoblast differentiation beyond the Runx2 stage (Rodda & McMahon, 2006). In mature bone, β-catenin in osteoblasts restrains osteoclast formation by raising osteoprotegerin (Glass et al., 2005), and the Wnt co-receptor LRP5 and the osteocyte-derived inhibitor sclerostin are major determinants of bone mass (Baron & Kneissel, 2013). In the face, Wnt/β-catenin activity marks and regulates regions of the developing facial prominences (Brugmann et al., 2007). Changes in Wnt target expression are therefore a plausible mechanism for a craniofacial or skeletal mutant phenotype.

1.2 TCF/LEF-dependent and TCF/LEF-independent β-catenin targets

Doumpas et al. (2019) used CRISPR/Cas9 to delete all four TCF/LEF genes (d4TCF) or β-catenin (dBcat) in HEK293T cells and stimulated each line with the GSK3 inhibitor CHIR99021 for 24 hours. Of 231 genes regulated by CHIR in parental cells, 166 did not respond in dBcat cells and were classed as β-catenin-dependent; the remaining 65 were β-catenin-independent, reflecting other effects of GSK3 inhibition. Of the 166 β-catenin-dependent genes, 139 lost their response in d4TCF cells (TCF/LEF-dependent), while 27 (about 15%) still responded (TCF/LEF-independent). The authors further described a "β-catenin-GHOST" response of about 90 genes regulated by β-catenin only when TCF/LEF are absent, and implicated FOXO4 in at least part of this programme, using GADD45 as an example.

These target classes provide a way to ask not only whether Wnt signalling is altered in a mutant tissue, but also which branch of β-catenin output is affected.

1.3 Aims

This report addresses three questions using the mutant versus control RNA-seq results:

  1. Which genes and gene programmes differ between mutant and control tissue?
  2. Are craniofacial, cartilage, osteoblast, osteocyte or osteoclast programmes shifted?
  3. Are the TCF/LEF-dependent or TCF/LEF-independent Wnt/β-catenin target classes of Doumpas et al. altered, and does the mutant response resemble β-catenin activation?

2. Materials and methods

2.1 Data

The primary input was a DESeq2 results table for a comparison of four mutant and four control mouse samples (file DESeq2_results_RECALCULATE_4control_4mutant-20251023_TM). It contains Ensembl gene identifiers, MGI symbols, the mean of normalised counts (baseMean), log2 fold change (mutant / control) and the raw Wald p-value for 22,444 genes. It does not contain adjusted p-values, standard errors or per-sample counts. A tab-separated copy of the same table was also available and was confirmed to be identical in content. The genotype, tissue, age and sex of the animals were not supplied with the data.

Wnt target lists were taken from Table EV1 of Doumpas et al. (2019), which gives, for each gene, the human symbol and the log2 fold change and p-value for CHIR treatment in wild-type, dBcat and d4TCF cells.

2.2 Pre-processing

Genes lacking a symbol (25) or a p-value (689, genes excluded by DESeq2's outlier or low-count filters) were removed. For 39 symbols present more than once, the row with the smallest p-value was retained, giving 21,715 genes. Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) false discovery rates were computed across these genes. These may differ slightly from DESeq2's own adjusted p-values, which apply independent filtering before adjustment.

2.3 Signed gene statistic

To rank genes by both direction and strength of change, each gene was assigned a signed z-statistic, z = sign(log2FC) × Φ⁻¹(1 − p/2), where Φ⁻¹ is the standard normal quantile function. This is the z-score that would give the observed two-sided p-value, carrying the sign of the fold change.

2.4 Gene sets

Paper-derived sets. Each of the four Table EV1 lists was split by the sign of its CHIR log2 fold change in wild-type cells, giving eight sets (for example "TCF/LEF-dependent, CHIR-induced"). Human symbols were matched to mouse symbols case-insensitively (for example AXIN2 to Axin2). This recovered 55–85% of each list; the unmatched genes were mostly lncRNAs, antisense transcripts and primate-specific genes (Table 1).

2.5 Gene set testing

Gene sets were tested with limma::cameraPR (Wu & Smyth, 2012), a competitive test that asks whether genes in a set have a more extreme statistic, on average, than the other genes. cameraPR corrects the test for correlation between genes in the set through a variance inflation factor, 1 + (m − 1)ρ, where m is the set size and ρ the inter-gene correlation. Because sample-level data were unavailable, ρ could not be estimated and was fixed at 0.01, the limma default. Sets with fewer than three genes were not tested. BH correction was applied across the tested sets.

2.6 Concordance with the published β-catenin response

For each Table EV1 list, the Spearman rank correlation between the CHIR log2 fold change in wild-type HEK293T cells and the mutant log2 fold change was computed. A positive correlation would indicate that the mutant resembles β-catenin activation; a negative one, β-catenin loss.

2.7 Why edgeR was not used for testing

edgeR models raw counts with a negative binomial generalised linear model, estimating a dispersion for each gene from the biological replicates (Robinson et al., 2010). This cannot be done from a table of fold changes and p-values. A complete edgeR quasi-likelihood pipeline (filterByExpr, TMM normalisation, estimateDisp, glmQLFit/glmQLFTest, glmTreat with a 1.5-fold threshold, and sample-level camera and fry tests) was therefore written and included in the repository, ready to run when counts are supplied.

2.8 Software and reproducibility

All analyses run from a single command (Rscript R/run_all.R) in R 4.6.1 with limma, edgeR 4.10.5 and readxl. Figures were produced with an equivalent implementation of the same steps; the R pipeline reproduced every reported gene count, p-value, FDR and median fold change exactly.

3. Results

3.1 The samples are mineralised bone

The most abundant transcripts were bone matrix and bone cell genes: Col1a1 (baseMean about 1.1 million), Col1a2 (0.9 million), Spp1 (141,000), Ctsk (44,000), Ibsp (24,000), Bglap (24,000), Acp5 (20,000) and Dmp1 (11,000). Osteoblasts, osteocytes and osteoclasts are therefore all represented. Epithelial markers were present at low levels (baseMean 35–400), indicating that a small amount of epithelium, such as oral, nasal or skin tissue, was carried into at least some samples. Y-chromosome genes (Ddx3y, Kdm5d, Eif2s3y, Uty) were expressed and not differentially expressed, and Xist was not present in the table, suggesting that male animals were used; this cannot be confirmed without per-sample counts.

3.2 Differential expression

Thirty genes passed FDR < 0.05: 25 were lower and 5 higher in the mutant (Figure 2, Table 3). The modest excess of small p-values (Figure 1) indicates a limited but genuine transcriptional difference, consistent with four replicates per group.

The downregulated genes fall into three groups. The first and largest is epithelial: keratins Krt5, Krt14 and Krt17, desmosome components Dsp, Pkp1 and Dsg2, and the epithelial surface genes Tacstd2 and Tmprss2, with decreases of 16- to 250-fold. Bpifb3, a secretory protein of airway and nasal epithelium, fell by about 1,000-fold. Other epithelial genes followed the same pattern at nominal significance, including Epcam (−4.4), Krt8 (−3.4), Irf6 (−3.2) and Cdh1 (−2.6). The second group consists of broadly expressed signalling and growth genes with small but highly significant decreases: Bmp6 (−0.73), Lama5 (−0.73), Mtor (−0.61) and Rgs5 (−0.92). The third is a pair of predicted genes, Gm6361 (−8.6) and Gm6565 (+8.5), which change by very large amounts in opposite directions.

The five upregulated genes were Gm6565, Il31ra (+3.4), Egr3 (+0.91), Zfp709 (+0.65) and Tarbp1 (+0.50).

Bone cells. The three bone cell programmes were all higher in the mutant, by a similar small amount (Table 4, Figure 4). In the osteoblast set, 29 of 34 genes were higher, and eight reached nominal significance: Spp1 (+1.01), Satb2 (+0.80), Col1a2 (+0.67), Sp7 (+0.65), Ank (+0.64), Bglap (+0.56) and Omd (+0.52), with Bmp6 the only significant gene moving the opposite way. All nine osteocyte genes were higher, led by Dmp1 (+1.02, p = 0.03) and Mepe (+1.07, p = 0.05); Sost was essentially unchanged (+0.27, p = 0.70). Fourteen of 16 osteoclast genes were higher, including Tnfsf11/RANKL (+0.72), Mmp9 (+0.51) and Ctsk (+0.40), but none reached nominal significance individually, and Tnfsf11 and its decoy receptor Tnfrsf11b/OPG (+0.46) rose together.

Cartilage. The cartilage set showed no overall shift, but contained individually changed genes in both directions: Col10a1, a marker of hypertrophic chondrocytes, was markedly lower (−4.1, p = 0.0008, low expression), as was Sox5 (−0.46, p = 0.02), while Col2a1 (+1.24, p = 0.045), Matn3 (+1.12, p = 0.02) and Col11a2 (+0.61, p = 0.03) were higher.

Craniofacial patterning. The craniofacial set as a whole was unchanged, but this average hid two distinct groups. Core mesenchymal patterning factors were stable, including Msx1 (+0.13), Msx2 (−0.23), Dlx5 (+0.30), Twist1 (+0.20) and Sox9 (−0.28). In contrast, several transcription factors were strongly lower at nominal significance: Pitx1 (−4.3, p = 7×10⁻⁴), Irf6 (−3.2, p = 9×10⁻⁵), Pax9 (−2.0, p = 0.04), Sox10 (−1.9, p = 0.006) and Tbx1 (−1.3, p = 4×10⁻⁴). None passed FDR < 0.05 genome-wide.

No Wnt target class was significantly shifted (all FDR ≥ 0.19; Table 5). The two sets of genes repressed by β-catenin in HEK293T cells trended slightly lower in the mutant (p = 0.07 and 0.09), which on its own would suggest mildly higher Wnt activity, but the corresponding induced sets showed no increase (median log2FC +0.02 and +0.04). The two trends therefore do not form a consistent picture of pathway activation.

The mutant fold changes were unrelated to the published CHIR response for every list (Figure 6): Spearman ρ = 0.07 for β-catenin-dependent genes (n = 120), 0.10 for TCF/LEF-dependent genes (n = 100), −0.21 for TCF/LEF-independent genes (n = 20) and 0.15 for β-catenin-independent genes (n = 49), all with p > 0.3.

At the level of individual genes, classic direct targets were unchanged: Axin2 (−0.30, p = 0.13), Lef1 (−0.01, p = 0.97), Nkd1 (−0.32, p = 0.29), Apcdd1 (−0.65, p = 0.16), Lgr5 (−0.91, p = 0.17), Dkk1 (+0.50, p = 0.26) and Wif1 (+0.66, p = 0.23); Sp5 was barely expressed. Notum was the only readout with a nominal change (+1.30, p = 0.03). The pathway components themselves were stable: Ctnnb1 (+0.18), Tcf7 (+0.58, p = 0.14), Tcf7l1 (+0.18), Tcf7l2 (+0.25) and Lef1. Among the genes linked by Doumpas et al. to the TCF/LEF-independent programme, Foxo1, Foxo3, Foxo4 (−0.37, p = 0.11) and Gadd45a/b/g were all unchanged.

3.5 Integrated view

Figure 7 summarises the pattern. The pathway core and its readouts are close to neutral, bone genes lean upward, and the strongest changes, both in the epithelial genes and in the craniofacial transcription factors Pitx1, Irf6, Pax9, Sox10 and Tbx1, are decreases. The figure adds no new statistical evidence; it is included as a visual summary of Tables 3–5.

4. Discussion

4.1 The epithelial signal most likely reflects tissue composition

The strongest and most coherent difference between groups was the loss of epithelial transcripts. Three features argue that this reflects how much epithelium was included in each sample rather than a transcriptional effect of the mutation in bone. First, the genes involved are not expressed by bone cells, and their low baseMean shows that epithelium is a minor component of the tissue. Second, the decreases are very large (16- to 1,000-fold) and span keratins, desmosomes, secretory proteins and epithelial transcription factors together, which is the signature of losing a cell type, not of regulating a pathway. Third, Bpifb3 and Tmprss2 point to airway or nasal epithelium, which is anatomically adjacent to craniofacial bone and easily included during dissection.

This interpretation also accounts for the strongest craniofacial changes. Irf6 is expressed in oral epithelium and is a major cleft lip and palate gene (Kondo et al., 2002), and Pitx1 and Pax9 are expressed in oral and pharyngeal epithelium as well as mesenchyme. Their decreases may therefore belong to the same composition effect, and should not be read as evidence of disrupted craniofacial patterning without confirmation. A genuine loss of epithelial tissue in the mutant, for example of a mucosal or glandular structure, cannot be excluded, and would itself be a phenotype worth describing. The two explanations make different predictions for the per-sample data: dissection variability would typically concentrate the epithelial signal in one or two control samples, whereas a true phenotype would separate the two groups consistently.

4.2 The bone signal: more bone, or more bone formation?

Osteoblast, osteocyte and osteoclast programmes were all higher in the mutant, by a similar amount of about 20–25% (log2FC +0.25 to +0.31). If each mutant sample simply contained a larger fraction of mineralised bone, and correspondingly less soft tissue such as epithelium, all bone-resident cell types would rise together, which is what was observed. A specific stimulation of bone formation would more typically raise osteoblast and osteocyte genes above osteoclast genes, and would be expected to involve the Wnt/β-catenin programme, which was unchanged. The uniform rise and the parallel increase of Tnfsf11 and Tnfrsf11b therefore favour composition. Nevertheless, a real increase in bone mass would also produce this pattern at the tissue level, so composition and biology are not mutually exclusive: a mutant with more bone would, by construction, yield samples richer in bone transcripts. Histology or micro-CT is needed to decide between these explanations.

4.3 Bmp6 is the most specific candidate

Bmp6 fell significantly (log2FC −0.73, FDR 1×10⁻⁴) while almost every other osteoblast gene rose. Because it runs against the composition trend, it is unlikely to be explained by tissue proportions, and it is the most specific transcriptional change in the bone data. BMP6 is an osteogenic BMP expressed by osteoblasts and hypertrophic chondrocytes, and BMP and Wnt signalling are closely coupled in bone formation. A reduction of about 40% in a secreted growth factor could alter local signalling without changing the bulk expression of its downstream targets, particularly over the short time window captured by a single tissue sample. Bmp6 should be prioritised for validation. Mtor (−0.61) and Lama5 (−0.73) behave similarly and are secondary candidates.

4.4 Absence of a Wnt/β-catenin signature

Neither the canonical TCF/LEF-dependent programme nor the TCF/LEF-independent programme described by Doumpas et al. was altered, and the mutant response showed no relationship to β-catenin activation. Several factors must be weighed before concluding that Wnt signalling is unaffected.

Transferability. The target classes were defined in human HEK293T cells after 24 hours of pharmacological GSK3 inhibition. Wnt target genes are strongly cell-type specific, and many HEK293T targets are unlikely to be expressed or Wnt-responsive in bone; indeed, 15–50% of each list could not be matched at all. The TCF/LEF-independent and GHOST classes were observed only after deleting all four TCF/LEF genes or blocking the TCF–β-catenin interaction with ICAT, conditions that are unlikely to arise in a mutant tissue unless the mutation targets that interaction directly. The universal readouts (Axin2, Nkd1, Lef1, Apcdd1) are the more appropriate test in this tissue, and they were also unchanged.

Dilution. In bulk bone, Wnt-responsive populations such as suture mesenchyme, periosteal progenitors or the osteoblast front form a small fraction of cells. A change confined to these cells can be diluted below detection, especially with four replicates per group.

Timing and compensation. Wnt target expression is dynamic. A mutation that alters signalling during development may leave little trace in the adult tissue sampled here, or may be compensated by feedback through Axin2, Dkk1 and Notum. The nominal rise in Notum, a Wnt-induced deacylase that inactivates Wnt ligands, is compatible with such feedback, but a single nominal change is not evidence for it.

Taken together, the data argue against a large, tissue-wide change in canonical Wnt/β-catenin transcription in this sample, but they do not exclude localised or developmental effects.

4.5 Other observations

The predicted genes Gm6361 and Gm6565 changed by several hundred-fold in opposite directions, with low expression. Such reciprocal changes in paralogous or pseudogene loci often arise from sequence differences between strains, for example around a targeted locus carried on a different genetic background, which redirect reads between near-identical sequences. They should be checked against the location of the mutation and the strain history before any biological interpretation. Col10a1 fell sharply at low expression, which may reflect variable inclusion of growth plate or synchondrosis cartilage, in line with the composition interpretation.

4.6 Strengths and limitations

The analysis has several strengths: it uses target classes defined independently in a published study, tests them with a method that accounts for inter-gene correlation, includes an explicit tissue-composition control, and is fully reproducible from a version-controlled repository. Its limitations are important:

  • No raw counts. Dispersion estimation, sample-level quality control and outlier detection were not possible, and the DESeq2 statistics had to be taken at face value.
  • Fixed inter-gene correlation. cameraPR with ρ = 0.01 underestimates the correlation within strongly co-regulated blocks, so the p-values for the epithelial and bone sets are overstated. They should be read as rankings of strength, not literal probabilities.
  • Ortholog matching. Case-insensitive symbol matching recovers most one-to-one orthologs but misses renamed genes and all non-coding transcripts.
  • Curated sets. The skeletal and craniofacial sets are expert-curated, not drawn from a database, and different choices would change individual results.
  • Missing metadata. Without the genotype, age, anatomical site and litter structure, several interpretations remain provisional.
  • Power. Four replicates per group can detect large or coordinated changes but not small effects in individual genes.

5. Conclusions

  1. The mutant and control samples are mineralised craniofacial or skeletal bone, and the transcriptional difference between them is modest (30 genes at FDR < 0.05).
  2. The largest difference is a coordinated loss of epithelial transcripts, most likely reflecting dissection or tissue composition, which may also account for the reduction in epithelially expressed craniofacial genes such as Irf6 and Pitx1.
  3. Osteoblast, osteocyte and osteoclast programmes are uniformly and modestly higher in the mutant, a pattern that fits a higher proportion of bone in the samples and may or may not reflect increased bone mass.
  4. Bmp6 is significantly reduced against the bone trend and is the most specific candidate for follow-up.
  5. There is no evidence of altered canonical, TCF/LEF-dependent Wnt/β-catenin transcription, and no evidence that TCF/LEF-independent β-catenin targets are engaged.

6. Recommended next steps

  1. Obtain the raw count matrix and sample metadata (genotype, sex, litter, age, anatomical site) and run the included edgeR pipeline. This provides dispersion-based testing, an MDS plot and sample-level camera/fry gene set tests.
  2. Resolve tissue composition. Plot per-sample expression of epithelial (Krt5, Krt14, Bpifb3) and bone (Col1a1, Bglap, Dmp1) markers. If the epithelial signal is driven by one or two samples, re-test with those samples removed or with an epithelial score as a covariate.
  3. Confirm the mutant allele in the counts and investigate the Gm6361/Gm6565 pair against the targeted locus and strain background.
  4. Run unbiased enrichment (limma::goana/kegga) and replace symbol matching with a curated ortholog table such as the MGI human–mouse homology report.
  5. Validate experimentally. Quantify Bmp6, Sp7, Dmp1, Spp1, Axin2 and Notum by RT-qPCR on independent samples, localise Wnt activity by Axin2 in situ hybridisation or reporter mice, and measure bone volume and cellularity by micro-CT and histomorphometry.
  6. If Wnt involvement remains a hypothesis, compare against Wnt target signatures defined in osteoblasts or craniofacial mesenchyme rather than HEK293T cells, or profile Wnt-responsive cells directly by single-cell RNA-seq.
